claim: As of March 2017, Sci-Hub's database contains 68.9% of the 81.6 million scholarly articles registered with Crossref.
source: Here we report that, as of March 2017, Sci-Hub's database contains 68.9% of the 81.6 million scholarly articles registered with Crossref and 85.1% of articles published in toll access journals.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis of Sci-Hub's DOI catalog released March 19, 2017 compared against Crossref database downloaded March 21, 2017.

claim: As of March 2017, Sci-Hub contains 85.1% of articles published in toll access journals.
source: Here we report that, as of March 2017, Sci-Hub's database contains 68.9% of the 81.6 million scholarly articles registered with Crossref and 85.1% of articles published in toll access journals.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis comparing Sci-Hub's catalog against toll access journals identified in the Scopus database.

claim: Sci-Hub provides greater coverage of toll access articles than the University of Pennsylvania.
source: For toll access articles, we find that Sci-Hub provides greater coverage than the University of Pennsylvania, a major research university in the United States.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of Sci-Hub's coverage with Penn Libraries' PennText access system on toll access articles.

claim: Nearly all scholarly literature is available gratis to anyone with an Internet connection.
source: For the first time, nearly all scholarly literature is available gratis to anyone with an Internet connection, suggesting the toll access business model may become unsustainable.
evidence: The claim is based on the finding that Sci-Hub contains 68.9% of all articles and 85.1% of toll access articles, combined with its ability to retrieve additional articles on demand.

claim: The toll access business model may become unsustainable.
source: For the first time, nearly all scholarly literature is available gratis to anyone with an Internet connection, suggesting the toll access business model may become unsustainable.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the inference that widespread gratis access via Sci-Hub threatens subscription-based publishing.

claim: Paywalls on the web limit access to three-quarters of scholarly literature.
source: Recent estimates suggest paywalls on the web limit access to three-quarters of scholarly literature (Piwowar et al., 2018; Khabsa et al., 2014; Bosman and Kramer, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Nearly 50% of newly published articles are available without paywalls.
source: After decades of effort by the open access community (Royster, 2016), nearly 50% of newly published articles are available without paywalls (Piwowar et al., 2018; Archambault et al., 2014; Van Noorden, 2013a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Smaller institutions or those in the developing world often have poor access to scholarly literature.
source: Smaller institutions or those in the developing world often have poor access to scholarly literature (Meadows, 2015; Kirsop and Chan, 2005; Bendezú-Quispe et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The price of journal subscriptions has grown at a faster rate than inflation for several decades.
source: As a result, the price of journal subscriptions has grown at a faster rate than inflation for several decades (Association of Research Libraries, 2017), leading to an ever-present "serials crisis" that has pushed library budgets to their brink while diverting funds from other services (Roth, 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research and reports.

claim: Publishing has trended towards oligopoly.
source: Meanwhile, publishing has trended towards oligopoly (Larivière et al., 2015), with nondisclosure clauses obfuscating price information among subscribers (Bergstrom et al., 2014) while publishers profit immensely (Morrison, 2012; Buranyi, 2017; Van Noorden, 2013b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Per-journal subscription costs increased by 25% from 2013–2017.
source: For example, EBSCO estimates that per-journal subscription costs increased by 25% from 2013–2017, with annual subscription to a journal for research libraries now averaging $1,396 (EBSCO, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to an EBSCO report.

claim: Sci-Hub was started in 2011 by Alexandra Elbakyan.
source: The website, started in 2011, is run by Alexandra Elbakyan, a graduate student and native of Kazakhstan who now resides in Russia (Bohannon, 2016a; Schiermeier, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published articles.

claim: Alexandra Elbakyan is motivated to provide universal access to knowledge.
source: Elbakyan describes herself as motivated to provide universal access to knowledge (Elbakyan, 2016a; Elbakyan, 2015; Milova, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to statements by Elbakyan.

claim: Sci-Hub retrieves and distributes scholarly literature without regard to copyright.
source: Sci-Hub does not restrict itself to only openly licensed content. Instead, it retrieves and distributes scholarly literature without regard to copyright.
evidence: This is a direct statement about Sci-Hub's operational approach.

claim: In many jurisdictions, use of Sci-Hub may constitute copyright infringement.
source: Readers should note that, in many jurisdictions, use of Sci-Hub may constitute copyright infringement.
evidence: This is a statement based on legal knowledge about copyright law.

claim: Sci-Hub uses leaked authentication credentials for educational institutions to bypass paywalls.
source: One method Sci-Hub uses to bypass paywalls is by obtaining leaked authentication credentials for educational institutions (Elbakyan, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Elbakyan's statement.

claim: Sci-Hub has experienced sustained growth since its inception.
source: Since its inception, Sci-Hub has experienced sustained growth, with spikes in interest and awareness driven by legal proceedings, service outages, news coverage, and social media (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1 showing Google Trends data over time.

claim: From the Spring of 2013 until the end of 2014, Sci-Hub relied on the Library Genesis (LibGen) scimag repository to store articles.
source: From the Spring of 2013 until the end of 2014, Sci-Hub relied on the Library Genesis (LibGen) scimag repository to store articles (Elbakyan, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Elbakyan's statement.

claim: At the start of 2014, LibGen contained 36% of all published scholarly articles.
source: Cabanac compared the number of articles in the LibGen scimag database at the start of 2014 to the total number of Crossref DOIs, estimating that LibGen contained 36% of all published scholarly articles (Cabanac, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Cabanac's research.

claim: LibGen's coverage in 2014 was 77% for Elsevier, 73% for Wiley, and 53% for Springer.
source: Coverage was higher for several prominent publishers: 77% for Elsevier, 73% for Wiley, and 53% for Springer (prior to its merger with Macmillan/Nature; Van Noorden, 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on Cabanac's analysis with additional citation for context.

claim: Portugal, Iran, Tunisia, and Greece had the highest per capita Sci-Hub usage.
source: Portugal, Iran, Tunisia, and Greece had the highest usage, suggesting Sci-Hub is preferentially used in countries with poor institutional access to scholarly literature.
evidence: The claim is based on Greshake's analysis of Sci-Hub access logs.

claim: Sci-Hub is preferentially used in countries with poor institutional access to scholarly literature.
source: Portugal, Iran, Tunisia, and Greece had the highest usage, suggesting Sci-Hub is preferentially used in countries with poor institutional access to scholarly literature.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of per capita usage.

claim: 12 of the top 20 most requested journals on Sci-Hub specialize in chemistry.
source: In a subsequent study, he found especially high Sci-Hub usage in chemistry, with 12 of the top 20 requested journals specializing in chemistry (Greshake, 2017a; Greshake, 2017b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Greshake's research.

claim: Since 2015, Sci-Hub has operated its own repository, distinct from LibGen.
source: Since 2015, Sci-Hub has operated its own repository, distinct from LibGen.
evidence: This is a statement about Sci-Hub's operational history.

claim: On March 19, 2017, Sci-Hub released the list of DOIs for articles in its database.
source: On March 19, 2017, Sci-Hub released the list of DOIs for articles in its database.
evidence: This is a factual statement about a specific event.

claim: 95% of articles in Sci-Hub were published after 1950.
source: He found that 95% of articles in Sci-Hub were published after 1950.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Greshake's analysis.

claim: Only 5% of Sci-Hub requests targeted articles published before 1983.
source: Sci-Hub requests were even more skewed towards recent articles, with only 5% targeting articles published before 1983.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Greshake's analysis.

claim: The scholarly literature consists of 81,609,016 texts identified by their DOIs.
source: We define the "scholarly literature" as 81,609,016 texts identified by their DOIs.
evidence: This is a definition based on data from the Crossref database.

claim: Sci-Hub's offerings included 56,246,220 articles from the corpus of scholarly literature.
source: Sci-Hub's offerings included 56,246,220 articles from the corpus of scholarly literature, equating to 68.9% of all articles.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of Sci-Hub's DOI catalog.

claim: Sci-Hub had 77.8% coverage of journal articles.
source: The scholarly literature consisted primarily of journal articles, for which Sci-Hub had 77.8% coverage.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Sci-Hub's coverage of proceedings articles was 79.7%.
source: Sci-Hub's coverage was also strong for the 5 million proceedings articles at 79.7%.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Sci-Hub's coverage of book chapters was poor at 14.2%.
source: Overall coverage suffered from the 10 million book chapters, where coverage was poor (14.2%).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The catalog consisted of 23,037 journals encompassing 56,755,671 articles.
source: Accordingly, our catalog consisted of 23,037 journals encompassing 56,755,671 articles.
evidence: This is a statement about the dataset derived from Scopus.

claim: 20.0% of journals in the catalog were inactive.
source: Of these journals, 4,598 (20.0%) were inactive (i.e. no longer publishing articles), and 2,933 were open access (12.7%).

claim: 12.7% of journals in the catalog were open access.
source: Of these journals, 4,598 (20.0%) were inactive (i.e. no longer publishing articles), and 2,933 were open access (12.7%).
evidence: This is a statistical summary of the journal catalog.

claim: Elsevier is the largest publisher with 13,115,639 articles from 3,410 journals.
source: The largest publisher was Elsevier, with 13,115,639 articles from 3,410 journals.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the publisher analysis.

claim: Sci-Hub covered 96.9% of Elsevier articles.
source: Sci-Hub covered 96.9% of Elsevier articles.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Sci-Hub covered 89.7% of Springer Nature articles.
source: For the eight publishers with more than one million articles, the following coverage was observed: 96.9% of Elsevier, 89.7% of Springer Nature, 94.7% of Wiley-Blackwell, 92.6% of Taylor & Francis, 79.4% of Wolters Kluwer, 88.3% of Oxford University Press, 90.9% of SAGE, and 98.8% of American Chemical Society articles.

source: For the eight publishers with more than one million articles, the following coverage was observed: 96.9% of Elsevier, 89.7% of Springer Nature, 94.7% of Wiley-Blackwell, 92.6% of Taylor & Francis, 79.4% of Wolters Kluwer, 88.3% of Oxford University Press, 90.9% of SAGE, and 98.8% of American Chemical Society articles.

claim: Sci-Hub covered 88.3% of Oxford University Press articles.
source: For the eight publishers with more than one million articles, the following coverage was observed: 96.9% of Elsevier, 89.7% of Springer Nature, 94.7% of Wiley-Blackwell, 92.6% of Taylor & Francis, 79.4% of Wolters Kluwer, 88.3% of Oxford University Press, 90.9% of SAGE, and 98.8% of American Chemical Society articles.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis of publisher coverage.

claim: Sci-Hub covered 90.9% of SAGE articles.
source: For the eight publishers with more than one million articles, the following coverage was observed: 96.9% of Elsevier, 89.7% of Springer Nature, 94.7% of Wiley-Blackwell, 92.6% of Taylor & Francis, 79.4% of Wolters Kluwer, 88.3% of Oxford University Press, 90.9% of SAGE, and 98.8% of American Chemical Society articles.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis of publisher coverage.

claim: Sci-Hub covered 98.8% of American Chemical Society articles.
source: For the eight publishers with more than one million articles, the following coverage was observed: 96.9% of Elsevier, 89.7% of Springer Nature, 94.7% of Wiley-Blackwell, 92.6% of Taylor & Francis, 79.4% of Wolters Kluwer, 88.3% of Oxford University Press, 90.9% of SAGE, and 98.8% of American Chemical Society articles.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis of publisher coverage.

claim: There is a dropoff in Sci-Hub coverage starting in 2010 for recently published articles.
source: However, there is a dropoff in coverage, starting in 2010, for recently published articles.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: 2016 coverage was 56.0%.
source: For example, 2016 coverage was 56.0% and 2017 coverage (for part of the year) was 45.3%.

source: For example, 2016 coverage was 56.0% and 2017 coverage (for part of the year) was 45.3%.
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis of coverage by year.

claim: Some publishers are deploying more aggressive measures to deter unauthorized article downloads.
source: Another possible factor is that some publishers are now deploying more aggressive measures to deter unauthorized article downloads (Rovner, 2014; Becker, 2016), making recent articles less accessible.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to reports about publisher anti-piracy measures.

claim: Sci-Hub's coverage of 2016 articles in open access journals was 32.7%.
source: Sci-Hub's coverage of 2016 articles in open access journals was just 32.7% compared to 78.8% for articles in toll access journals (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sci-Hub's coverage of 2016 articles in toll access journals was 78.8%.
source: Sci-Hub's coverage of 2016 articles in open access journals was just 32.7% compared to 78.8% for articles in toll access journals (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In June 2015, Sci-Hub ceased archiving articles in PeerJ, eLife, and PLOS journals.
source: Upon further investigation, we discovered that in June 2015, Sci-Hub ceased archiving articles in PeerJ, eLife, and PLOS journals, although they continued archiving articles in other open access journals such as Scientific Reports, Nature Communications, and BMC-series journals.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' investigation of Sci-Hub's archiving behavior.

claim: Sci-Hub prioritizes circumventing access barriers rather than creating a single repository containing every scholarly article.
source: These findings suggest Sci-Hub prioritizes circumventing access barriers rather than creating a single repository containing every scholarly article.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of selective archiving.

claim: Sci-Hub's coverage of gold articles was 49.2%.
source: In line with our findings on the entire Crossref article catalog where Sci-Hub covered 49.1% of articles in open access journals, Sci-Hub's coverage of gold articles in the State of OA dataset was 49.2%.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Sci-Hub's coverage of closed articles was 90.4%.
source: Coverage of the 165,340 closed articles was 90.4%.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Sci-Hub's coverage was higher for closed and green articles than for hybrid or bronze articles.
source: Sci-Hub's coverage was higher for closed and green articles than for hybrid or bronze articles.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Users resort to Sci-Hub after encountering a paywall but before checking oaDOI or a search engine for green access.
source: These findings suggest a historical pattern where users resort to Sci-Hub after encountering a paywall but before checking oaDOI or a search engine for green access.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the coverage patterns across access categories.

claim: The University of Pennsylvania is a private research university located in Philadelphia and founded by Benjamin Franklin in 1749.
source: Penn is a private research university located in Philadelphia and founded by the open science pioneer Benjamin Franklin in 1749.
evidence: This is a statement of historical fact.

claim: Penn has an endowment of over $10 billion.
source: It is one of the world's wealthiest universities, with an endowment of over $10 billion.
evidence: This is a factual statement about Penn's financial resources.

claim: R&D expenditures at Penn totaled $1.29 billion in 2016.
source: According to the Higher Education Research and Development Survey, R&D expenditures at Penn totaled $1.29 billion in 2016, placing it third among U.S. colleges and universities.
evidence: This is a factual statement based on survey data.

claim: In 2017, Penn Libraries spent $13.13 million on electronic resources.
source: In 2017, Penn Libraries estimates that it spent $13.13 million on electronic resources, which includes subscriptions to journals and ebooks.
evidence: This is a factual statement based on Penn Libraries data.

claim: Penn Libraries users accessed 7.3 million articles in 2017.
source: During this year, its users accessed 7.3 million articles and 860 thousand ebook chapters, averaging a per-download cost of $1.61.
evidence: This is a factual statement based on Penn Libraries usage data.

claim: The average per-download cost at Penn Libraries was $1.61.
source: During this year, its users accessed 7.3 million articles and 860 thousand ebook chapters, averaging a per-download cost of $1.61.
evidence: This is calculated from the spending and usage data.

claim: PennText correctly classified access 88.2% of the time.
source: Using these manual access calls, we found PennText correctly classified access 88.2% [85.2%–90.8%] of the time (bracketed ranges refer to 95% confidence intervals calculated using Jeffreys interval for binomial proportions (Rubin and Schenker, 1987)).
evidence: The claim is based on manual evaluation of 500 articles.

claim: 34.8% of articles were accessible from their publisher's site without institutional access.
source: Based on our manual evaluation of 500 articles, we found 34.8% [30.7%–39.1%] of articles were accessible this way.
evidence: The claim is based on manual evaluation of 500 articles.

claim: oaDOI provided access to 15.3% of toll access articles.
source: oaDOI — a utility that redirects paywalled DOIs to gratis, licit versions, when possible (Piwowar et al., 2018) — was able to access 15.3% [11.7%–19.5%] of these toll access articles, indicating that green open access is still limited in its reach.
evidence: The claim is based on manual evaluation of 326 toll access articles.

claim: Green open access is still limited in its reach.
source: oaDOI — a utility that redirects paywalled DOIs to gratis, licit versions, when possible (Piwowar et al., 2018) — was able to access 15.3% [11.7%–19.5%] of these toll access articles, indicating that green open access is still limited in its reach.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the low percentage of toll access articles available via oaDOI.

claim: Sci-Hub and Penn had similar coverage on all articles: 85.2% versus 87.4% on the manual article set.
source: Sci-Hub and Penn had similar coverage on all articles: 85.2% [81.9%–88.1%] versus 87.4% [84.3%–90.1%] on the manual article set and 84.8% [84.7%–84.9%] versus 84.4% [84.3%–84.5%] on the larger but automated set.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: When considering only toll access articles, Sci-Hub's coverage exceeds Penn's: 94.2% versus 80.7% on the manual set.
source: However, when considering only toll access articles, Sci-Hub's coverage exceeds Penn's: 94.2% [91.2%–96.3%] versus 80.7% [76.1%–84.7%] on the manual set and 90.7% [90.5%–90.8%] versus 83.5% [83.4%–83.7%] on the automated set.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Sci-Hub provided greater access to paywalled articles than a leading research university spending millions of US dollars per year on subscriptions.
source: Remarkably, Sci-Hub provided greater access to paywalled articles than a leading research university spending millions of US dollars per year on subscriptions.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the comparison of Sci-Hub and Penn coverage.

claim: Together, Sci-Hub's repository and Penn's access covered approximately 96% of toll access articles.
source: Together, Sci-Hub's repository and Penn's access covered approximately 96% of toll access articles [95.0%–98.6% (manual set), 95.9%–96.1% (automated set)].
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Users with institutional subscriptions comparable to Penn as well as knowledge of oaDOI and Sci-Hub are able to access over 97% of all articles.
source: Our findings suggest that users with institutional subscriptions comparable to those at Penn as well as knowledge of oaDOI and Sci-Hub are able to access over 97% of all articles [96.7%–99.1% (manual set), 97.3%–97.5% (automated set)], online and without payment.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: 6,657,410 of recent citations (91.0%) referenced an article that was in Sci-Hub.
source: 6,657,410 of the recent citations (91.0%) referenced an article that was in Sci-Hub.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of citations from articles published since 2015.

claim: Sci-Hub covered 96.2% of recent citations to articles in toll access journals.
source: However, if only considering the 6,264,257 citations to articles in toll access journals, Sci-Hub covered 96.2% of recent citations.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of citations to toll access articles.

claim: For citations to articles in open access journals, Sci-Hub covered only 62.3%.
source: On the other hand, for the 866,115 citations to articles in open access journals, Sci-Hub covered only 62.3%.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of citations to open access articles.

claim: Sci-Hub released article access records covering 165 days from September 2015 through February 2016.
source: Sci-Hub released article access records from its server logs, covering 165 days from September 2015 through February 2016 (Elbakyan and Bohannon, 2016; Bohannon, 2016b).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the access log data release.

claim: The logs contained 26,984,851 access events.
source: After processing, the logs contained 26,984,851 access events.
evidence: This is a statement about the processed log data.

claim: Sci-Hub provided access to an average of 164,000 valid requests per day in late 2015–early 2016.
source: Hence, Sci-Hub provided access to an average of 164,000 valid requests per day in late 2015–early 2016.
evidence: This is calculated from the log data.

claim: All requests in Sci-Hub access logs are resolved requests where the user successfully downloaded a PDF.
source: Fortunately, Sci-Hub reviewed the preprint in a series of tweets, and pointed out the error, stating "in Sci-Hub access logs released previous year, all requests are resolved requests, i.e. user successfully downloaded PDF with that DOI … unresolved requests are not saved".
evidence: This is a clarification provided by Sci-Hub about the nature of the log data.

claim: Articles from toll access journals averaged 1.30 visitors.
source: In aggregate, articles from toll access journals averaged 1.30 visitors, whereas articles from open access journals averaged 0.25 visitors.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the Sci-Hub access logs.

claim: Articles from open access journals averaged 0.25 visitors.
source: In aggregate, articles from toll access journals averaged 1.30 visitors, whereas articles from open access journals averaged 0.25 visitors.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the Sci-Hub access logs.

claim: Articles in toll access journals received many times more visitors than those in open access journals, even after accounting for journal impact.
source: In addition, Figure 9B shows that articles in toll access journals received many times more visitors than those in open access journals, even after accounting for journal impact.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Sci-Hub's repository contained 69% of all scholarly articles with DOIs.
source: Sci-Hub's repository contained 69% of all scholarly articles with DOIs.
evidence: This is a summary of the main coverage finding.

claim: Coverage for the 54.5 million articles attributed to toll access journals was 85.1%.
source: Coverage for the 54.5 million articles attributed to toll access journals — which many users would not otherwise be able to access — was 85.1%.
evidence: This is a summary of the toll access coverage finding.

claim: Sci-Hub can retrieve, in real time, requested articles that are not in its database.
source: Since Sci-Hub can retrieve, in real time, requested articles that are not in its database, our coverage figures are a lower bound.
evidence: This is a statement about Sci-Hub's operational capability.

claim: Sci-Hub preferentially covered popular, paywalled articles.
source: Furthermore, Sci-Hub preferentially covered popular, paywalled articles.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the coverage patterns and access log analysis.

claim: Journals with very low coverage tended to be obscure, less cited venues.
source: Journals with very low (including zero) coverage tended to be obscure, less cited venues, while average coverage of the most cited journals exceeded 90%.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of coverage by journal impact.

claim: Average coverage of the most cited journals exceeded 90%.
source: Journals with very low (including zero) coverage tended to be obscure, less cited venues, while average coverage of the most cited journals exceeded 90%.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 9A.

claim: There is strong evidence that Sci-Hub is primarily used to circumvent paywalls.
source: We find strong evidence that Sci-Hub is primarily used to circumvent paywalls.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including access patterns and coverage by access status.

claim: Users accessed articles from toll access journals much more frequently than open access journals.
source: In particular, users accessed articles from toll access journals much more frequently than open access journals.
evidence: This is a finding from the access log analysis.

claim: Sci-Hub provided higher coverage of articles in the closed and green categories as opposed to the hybrid and bronze categories.
source: Additionally, within toll access journals, Sci-Hub provided higher coverage of articles in the closed and green categories (paywalled by the publisher) as opposed to the hybrid and bronze categories (available gratis from the publisher).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of coverage by access status.

claim: Many users likely only resort to Sci-Hub when access through a commercial database is cumbersome or costly.
source: Accordingly, many users likely only resort to Sci-Hub when access through a commercial database is cumbersome or costly.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the usage patterns.

claim: Sci-Hub's primary operational focus is circumventing paywalls rather than compiling all literature.
source: Finally, we observed evidence that Sci-Hub's primary operational focus is circumventing paywalls rather than compiling all literature, as archiving was deactivated in 2015 for several journals that exemplify openness.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the selective archiving behavior.

claim: Sci-Hub's database already contains more toll access articles than are immediately accessible via the University of Pennsylvania.
source: Attesting to its success in this mission, Sci-Hub's database already contains more toll access articles than are immediately accessible via the University of Pennsylvania, a leading research university.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparison of Sci-Hub and Penn coverage.

claim: Many users appear to value Sci-Hub's service, judging from donations.
source: Judging from donations, many users appear to value Sci-Hub's service.

source: Now however, Sci-Hub only advertises donation via Bitcoin, presumably to avoid banking blockades or government seizure of funds.
evidence: This is a statement about Sci-Hub's current donation methods.

source: We find that, prior to 2018, these addresses have received 1,232 donations, totaling 94.494 (Figure 10).

claim: 85.467 bitcoins have been withdrawn from the Sci-Hub addresses via 174 transactions.
source: 85.467 bitcoins have been withdrawn from the Sci-Hub addresses via 174 transactions.

claim: The combined US dollar value of withdrawals at time of withdrawal was $421,272.
source: Since the price of bitcoins has risen, the combined US dollar value at time of withdrawal was $421,272.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of Bitcoin blockchain data.

claim: At the conclusion of 2017, the Sci-Hub accounts had an outstanding balance of 9.027 bitcoins, valued at roughly $120,000.
source: At the conclusion of 2017, the Sci-Hub accounts had an outstanding balance of 9.027 bitcoins, valued at roughly $120,000.

claim: Elsevier filed suit against Sci-Hub.
source: Elsevier (whose 13.5 million works are 96.9% covered by Sci-Hub) and the American Chemical Society (whose 1.4 million works are 98.8% covered) both filed suit against Sci-Hub, despite the limited enforcement options of United States courts.
evidence: This is a statement of fact about legal action.

claim: The American Chemical Society filed suit against Sci-Hub.
source: Elsevier (whose 13.5 million works are 96.9% covered by Sci-Hub) and the American Chemical Society (whose 1.4 million works are 98.8% covered) both filed suit against Sci-Hub, despite the limited enforcement options of United States courts.
evidence: This is a statement of fact about legal action.

claim: The widespread gratis access that Sci-Hub provides to previously paywalled articles calls into question the sustainability of the subscription publishing model.
source: The widespread gratis access that Sci-Hub provides to previously paywalled articles calls into question the sustainability of the subscription publishing model (McKenzie, 2017; Lawson, 2017b).

claim: Avoiding biblioleaks and retaining exclusive possession of digital media may prove an insurmountable challenge for publishers.
source: Avoiding biblioleaks and retaining exclusive possession of digital media may prove an insurmountable challenge for publishers (Dunn et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by citation.

claim: Successors to Sci-Hub may emerge that no longer rely on a centralized service as distributed and censorship-resistant file storage protocols mature.
source: As distributed and censorship-resistant file storage protocols mature (Benet, 2014; ConsenSys, 2016), successors to Sci-Hub may emerge that no longer rely on a centralized service.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about future developments.

claim: Alexandra Elbakyan is only one individual in the larger "guerilla access" movement.

evidence: This is a statement about the broader context of shadow libraries supported by citations.

claim: Sci-Hub's corpus of gratis scholarly literature may be extremely difficult to suppress.

source: Surveys from 2016 suggest awareness and usage of Sci-Hub was not yet commonplace (Travis, 2016; Mejia et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to survey research.

claim: Adoption of Sci-Hub appears to be growing.
source: However, adoption appears to be growing.

source: According to Elbakyan, the number of Sci-Hub downloads increased from 42 million in 2015 to 75 million in 2016, equating to a 79% gain (Van Noorden, 2016).

claim: Sci-Hub averaged 185,243 downloads per day in January–February 2016.
source: As per Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Sci-Hub averaged 185,243 downloads per day in January–February 2016, whereas in 2017 daily downloads averaged 458,589.

source: As per Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Sci-Hub averaged 185,243 downloads per day in January–February 2016, whereas in 2017 daily downloads averaged 458,589.

claim: The ratio of Sci-Hub to Penn Libraries downloads in 2017 was 20:1.

source: University of Montreal reduced its subscriptions to Taylor & Francis periodicals by 93%, axing 2,231 journals (Gagnon, 2017).

claim: Growing Sci-Hub usage could become both the cause and the effect of dwindling subscriptions.
source: In the worst case for toll access publishers, growing Sci-Hub usage will become both the cause and the effect of dwindling subscriptions.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential future dynamics.

claim: Sci-Hub could decrease the use of library subscriptions as many users find it more convenient than authorized access.
source: Sci-Hub could decrease the use of library subscriptions as many users find it more convenient than authorized access (Travis, 2016).

source: The posting of preprints and postprints has been growing rapidly (Piwowar et al., 2018; Kaiser, 2017), with new search tools to help locate them (Singh Chawla, 2017c).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Scholarly publishers may have already lost the access battle.
source: In essence, scholarly publishers may have already lost the access battle.

claim: Publishers will be forced to adapt quickly to open access publishing models.
source: Publishers will be forced to adapt quickly to open access publishing models.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about future publisher behavior.

claim: Sci-Hub is poised to fundamentally disrupt scholarly publishing.
source: Sci-Hub is poised to fundamentally disrupt scholarly publishing.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the findings about Sci-Hub's coverage and usage.

claim: The transition to gratis availability of scholarly articles is currently underway.
source: The transition to gratis availability of scholarly articles is currently underway, and such a model may be inevitable in the long term (Lewis, 2012; Sutton, 2011; Jha, 2012).
evidence: This is a claim about current trends supported by citations.

claim: Gratis availability of scholarly articles may be inevitable in the long term.
source: The transition to gratis availability of scholarly articles is currently underway, and such a model may be inevitable in the long term (Lewis, 2012; Sutton, 2011; Jha, 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by citations.

claim: Only libre access, enabled by open licensing, allows building applications on top of scholarly literature without fear of legal consequences.
source: Only libre access, enabled by open licensing, allows building applications on top of scholarly literature without fear of legal consequences (Himmelstein, 2016).

claim: The barriers to fulltext mining are legal, not technological.

claim: DOIs are case-insensitive within the ASCII character range.
source: An often overlooked aspect of the DOI system is that DOIs are case-insensitive within the ASCII character range (International DOI Foundation, 2017; British Standards Institute, 2012).

claim: Around 90% of newly published articles in the sciences have DOIs.
source: By evaluating the presence of DOIs in other databases of scholarly literature (such as PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus), researchers estimate around 90% of newly published articles in the sciences have DOIs (Gorraiz et al., 2016; Boudry and Chartron, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: DOI assignment in newly published Arts & Humanities articles is around 60%.
source: The prevalence of DOIs varies by discipline and country of publication, with DOI assignment in newly published Arts & Humanities articles around 60% (Gorraiz et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Crossref has registered 67% of all DOIs in existence.
